species: mouse (in vivo brain stimulation); rat (ex vivo retina)
readout_other: Multi-electrode array (MEA) recording of retinal ganglion cell extracellular potentials; electromyography (EMG) from mouse tail muscle; video recording of tail motion response
direction_notes: Ultrasound stimulation excited retinal ganglion cells (responses at stimulus onset and offset) and evoked tail-flick motor responses (via EMG and video) in mice, both indicating an activating effect.

exposures.label: In vivo mouse brain (tail motor area) stimulation

target.label: The targeted region was located 4.0 mm anteroposteriorally and 3.5 mm laterally from the bregma

timing.protocol_description: The ultrasonic transducer was fixed on the mouse's head by a stereotaxic frame; ultrasonic gel was used for coupling and the target could be adjusted in three dimensions with a 0.01 mm step. The reaction of the mouse to brain stimulation (evoked by ultrasound stimulating bursts, 1 MHz transducer) was recorded by an EMG acquisition system from the tail muscle and by video; the tail flicked when the ultrasound stimulus was on and stayed still when off. Full acoustic timing and intensity parameters used for this in vivo demonstration are not stated; animal preparation and experimental details were referred to another publication.

exposures.label: Ex vivo rat retina stimulation (MEA recording)

target.label: isolated rat retina, retinal ganglion cells facing the electrode array

timing.protocol_description: Rat retinas were prepared and a small patch of retina was placed into a recording chamber with retinal ganglion cells facing a 120-electrode MEA, used to detect extracellular potentials. The transducer was placed right above the retina to achieve ultrasound stimulation, performed under dim red light. Recorded responses over 12 successive trials showed the retinal ganglion cell was reliably excited by both the onset and offset of each stimulus. The frequency, timing, and intensity parameters used for this ex vivo demonstration are not stated in the text.

source_quotes.exposures[0].fundamental_frequency_khz: Fig. 10(a) shows the synchronous EMG signals, which were recorded from the tail muscle of a mouse, evoked by ultrasound stimulating bursts (1 MHz transducer). The targeted region was located 4.0 mm anteroposteriorally and 3.5 mm laterally from the bregma.
source_quotes.exposures[0].device.manufacturer: The bandwidth of the transducer was tested by a pulser-receiver (5800PR, Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) and a polished steel reflector.

flags.reason: Full acoustic timing (pulse duration, PRF, duty cycle, sonication duration) and intensity/pressure actually used for the in vivo mouse brain stimulation demonstration are not stated; the paper refers to methods described in another publication [Tufail et al., 2010]. General bench characterization of the same 1 MHz transducer (peak pressure 258 kPa in a separate water-tank scan, Fig. 8a) is not explicitly linked to this in vivo experiment, so it was not assigned here.

Neither the transducer/frequency (1 MHz commercial vs 3 MHz PMN-PT custom) nor any timing/intensity parameters are stated for the ex vivo retina stimulation experiment. The Discussion notes the miniaturized transducer 'would be useful for...MEA based physiological experiment', which may imply it was used, but this is not stated as fact in the Results.
The paper reports single demonstrative examples (e.g., 'a mouse', 'a retinal ganglion cell (one channel)') without stating the total number of animals or retinal preparations used.

This paper is primarily a device/engineering description with two brief, differently-scaled demonstration experiments (ex vivo rat retina via MEA, and in vivo mouse brain via EMG/video); top-level subject fields (n_subjects, subject_unit, anaesthesia, etc.) cannot fully represent both preparations simultaneously.
